summary: Pupils aged 11–14 learn to represent direct proportion across three linked views — a double number line (two parallel scales aligned at 0), a ratio table in which every kg entry is multiplied by the same constant to give its £ entry, and a coordinate graph whose signature is a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN. The core insight is that the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (e.g. 1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6), the kg-to-£ multiplier in each pair in the table, and the gradient of the line (£ per kg) are ONE AND THE SAME constant multiplier. Learners plot proportional pairs and draw the line, explain why it must pass through (0,0) (zero of one quantity means zero of the other), and read off unknowns (if 3 kg costs £6, find 5 kg → £10). The persistent error to confront is treating any straight or rising line as proportional while ignoring the origin.
misconceptions: Thinking any straight line — or any rising graph — shows direct proportion, ignoring whether it passes through the origin.
Not aligning the double number line at 0, so equivalent ratios don't correspond.
Reading a graph as isolated points and being unable to interpolate an unknown, or swapping the axes when reading off.
Believing the graph need not start at (0,0) — missing that zero of one quantity means zero of the other.

activities.title: Linked board: one rate, three views that move together
steps: Enter or accept a rate such as 3 kg → £6 and watch a ratio table, a double number line, and a coordinate graph populate for the SAME example.
Plot the proportional pairs on the graph and draw the line; confirm it passes through the origin.
Drag a point to 5 kg and read £10 simultaneously on the table, the number line, and the graph.

Point to where the constant '×2' appears in each view: the gradient of the line (£2 per kg), the multiplier from each kg entry to its £ entry in the table (3 → 6, 5 → 10), and the factor linking each pair of matching marks on the double number line (1 kg ↔ £2, 3 kg ↔ £6).
Flip a 'fixed charge' toggle (e.g. add a standing £2) and observe the whole line lift OFF the origin while staying perfectly straight; state whether it is still proportional and why not.
activities.insight: All three representations encode the SAME constant multiplier, and the origin — not mere straightness — is the test of proportionality.

activities.title: Annotated proportion graph: reveal the origin, the rate, and a read-off
steps: Examine a proportion graph and reveal, at the origin, that 'at 0 kg, cost is £0'.
Reveal along the line the constant multiplier (the rate, e.g. £2/kg).
Reveal at a chosen point its read-off (e.g. 5 kg → £10).
Compare a companion line that is straight but does NOT pass through the origin (a fixed £2 charge plus £2/kg) and decide, with reasons, that it is not proportional.
activities.insight: The recognition cues of a proportional graph are the origin crossing and a single constant rate; a straight line that misses the origin is a direct counterexample to 'straight means proportional'.

activities.title: Identify, read, and produce proportional lines
steps: Choose which of several graphs shows direct proportion, where a straight not-through-origin line is a deliberate trap.
Given a ratio table, plot the points and draw the matching line through the origin.
Read an unknown off a line through (3,6) (e.g. find the cost of 5 kg → £10), stating which axis you read up from and which you read across to.

On the same axes, DRAW a line for a DIFFERENT fruit's price: note that a £2/kg fruit would COINCIDE with the given £2/kg line through (3,6), whereas a shallower £1/kg line passes through (3,3) — and check your line is anchored at the origin.
activities.insight: Interpreting a point, interpolating an unknown, and independently producing an origin-anchored line together show whether the learner sees the graph as a constant-multiplier relationship rather than a picture.

checkQuestion: Here is a graph: a straight line through the origin passing through the point (3, 6), where the x-axis is weight in kg and the y-axis is cost in pounds. (a) What does the point (3, 6) tell you? (b) Use the line to find the cost of 5 kg. (c) Now, on the same axes, DRAW the line for a different fruit that costs £2 per kg.
checkAnswer: (a) 3 kg costs £6 (so this fruit is £2 per kg). (b) 5 kg costs £10 — read up from 5 on the x-axis to the line and across to £10. (c) A straight line through the origin passing through (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6)… — in fact the SAME line here, since £2/kg matches; if asked for, say £1/kg would be a shallower line through the origin, e.g. (3, 3).
